documents.title: Guidelines for Using Generative AI at App State
documents.summary: The App State AI site asks users to follow existing policies, vet tools before using university data, take full responsibility for output and disclose use. It does not say whether students may use AI in courses; faculty are asked to set expectations in syllabi.
documents.stance_why: It "encourages safe exploration" of AI but sets no student rule: it says "Students are expected to abide by the Academic Integrity Code" and "Faculty are asked to communicate clear expectations to students", so course-level decisions go to instructors.

units.why: The opening says the guidelines "will change as more work around this topic takes place", a statement that the policy is provisional, so it is a governance/over-time item (P54) addressed to all, informing only.
units.anchor: These guidelines for AI use will change as more work around this topic takes place

units.why: "App State encourages safe exploration and use of generative AI tools" is the institution welcoming AI use by everyone, so it is the default permit/encourage stance (P02), phrased as encouragement, not a duty.
units.anchor: App State encourages safe exploration and use of generative AI tools
units.frag_end: teaching, learning, research and other pursuits.

units.why: "The use of AI tools must adhere to existing policies" sets the institution-wide framework (P56) that binds all users to current policies and law; it is a must but takes no position on whether AI is allowed.
units.anchor: The use of AI tools must adhere to existing policies

units.why: "Students are expected to abide by the Academic Integrity Code" ties student AI use to the existing integrity code; it does not name AI misconduct itself, so P56 (framework) fits better than P36.
units.anchor: Students are expected to abide by the Academic Integrity Code

units.why: "Faculty are asked to communicate clear expectations to students on generative AI use in their courses" asks instructors to state AI expectations in their courses (P09), pushing the decision to them.
units.anchor: Faculty are asked to communicate clear expectations to students on generative AI use

units.why: Use of university information with AI is allowed "only when" the tool has been reviewed and contracts protect data, i.e. restricted to vetted tools (P50); it addresses faculty, students and staff alike.
units.anchor: only when: The AI tool or service being used has undergone appropriate internal reviews

units.why: "Adhere to ethical and legal standards and norms of the disciplines and the university, with regard to data privacy, consent, ownership and academic integrity" is a general principle for all users (P56) rather than a specific rule.
units.anchor: Adhere to ethical and legal standards and norms of the disciplines and the university

units.why: The Office of Research and Innovation pointing researchers to guidelines on "laws, rules and policies governing research" defers AI in research to a separate rulebook (P62).
units.anchor: The Office of Research and Innovation has published guidelines

units.why: "You are 100% responsible for the output you use" makes users own whatever AI output they use, which is P29 (own what you submit); it is addressed to all users.
units.anchor: You are 100% responsible for the output you use.

units.why: AI content "may be biased, inaccurate, completely fabricated" and so requires "thorough human review prior to use"; this is verify-the-output (P31), chosen over P29 because the explicit instruction is to review.
units.anchor: therefore requiring thorough human review prior to use

units.why: The same sentence warns that content may "contain copyright-protected or proprietary information", a licensing/IP concern (P52) distinct from the accuracy warning, so coded separately.
units.anchor: contain copyright-protected or proprietary information
units.policy: Generative AI-produced content may contain copyright-protected or proprietary information.

units.why: "The use of generative AI ... should be clearly documented and disclosed" asks for disclosure of AI use in university-related work (P24); "should" makes it a recommendation.
units.anchor: should be clearly documented and disclosed

documents.unit: Provost's Task Force on AI (Teaching and Learning)
documents.title: Initial Recommendations on Generative AI Policy and Philosophy (AI syllabus guidance)
documents.summary: A Provost task force sets seven principles and guidelines for instructors deciding how or whether students use AI, followed by sample syllabus statements sorted into permissive, restrictive and mixed. It sets no rule and recommends none of the samples.
documents.stance_why: The document says "the continuously evolving nature of AI defies any hard and fast rules" and "Do not assume/apply a one-size fits all policy", offers sample statements in permissive/restrictive/mixed groups and says it "does not recommend any one of the following samples".

units.why: The purpose section says the document "does not include recommendations about how instructors should use AI in their teaching practices", which fixes its scope (P61) to student AI use in assignments.
units.anchor: include recommendations about how instructors should use AI in their teaching practices

units.why: The task force observes that "appropriate student use of AI varies significantly from one academic discipline to another" and therefore leaves decisions to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: use of AI varies significantly from one academic discipline to another
units.frag_end: they bring to the task of teaching.

units.why: "the continuously evolving nature of AI defies any hard and fast rules for its governance" states the guidance is provisional (P54) rather than setting fixed rules.
units.anchor: nature of AI defies any hard and fast rules for its governance

units.why: Principle 1 Guideline 1 tells instructors to define "how and when students can use AI in your class" and put it in the syllabus; this is the syllabus-statement duty (P09), with the instruction to explain why.
units.anchor: Be proactive in clearly defining how and when students can use AI in
units.policy: Instructors define how and when students can use AI in the class, including why AI may be appropriate in some instances and not in others, state this in the syllabus and discuss it with the class at the start of the semester.

units.why: Guideline 2 asks instructors to "Align your AI use policy with your pedagogical values", leaving the policy to the instructor (P04), and warns a no-use policy may not fit a value of student agency.
units.anchor: Align your AI use policy with your pedagogical values, goals, and

units.why: The Texas A&M sample says using an AI generator "without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty", classing unauthorized AI use as misconduct (P36); it is a sample statement, not the university's own rule.
units.anchor: without proper attribution or authorization is a form of academic dishonesty

units.why: The sample tells students unsure about plagiarism to "contact your instructor to discuss the issue", i.e. ask before acting (P10).
units.anchor: please contact your instructor to discuss the issue

units.why: The note that AI violations "are typically cited as 'unauthorized assistance'" under the Academic Integrity Code, Article V 5.01 Cheating, says AI misuse is handled as cheating (P36).
units.anchor: AI violations are typically cited as
units.policy: AI violations are typically cited as "unauthorized assistance" under 5.01 Cheating in Article V, Prohibited Academic Conduct, of the Academic Integrity Code.

units.why: Principle 2 says to "Promote transparency and accountability in the use, reporting, and citing of AI", a general call for disclosure of AI use (P24) addressed to instructors who design the class.
units.anchor: Promote transparency and accountability in the use, reporting, and citing of AI.

units.why: "stating how faculty might use AI-detection tools in assessing students' work" asks faculty to tell students about their own AI use in assessment (P47), chosen over P40 because the point is disclosure.
units.anchor: stating how faculty might use AI-detection tools in assessing students

units.why: Guideline 1 asks instructors to "Establish open lines of communication" so students "talk to instructors" before using AI, i.e. ask first (P10).
units.anchor: they feel inclined to use AI on assignments

units.why: Guideline 2 asks for a "collegial conversation about how they produced the work", a conversation where students explain their work and AI's role (P34).
units.anchor: Engage students in a collegial conversation about how they produced

units.why: Guideline 3 says to "Disclose any intended use of AI in the assessment of student work", instructor disclosure of AI use in grading (P47).
units.anchor: Disclose any intended use of AI in the assessment of student work

units.why: The same guideline asks instructors to have students "opt in or out" of having work "added to a public database", a student-data choice (P50) rather than a disclosure rule.
units.anchor: ask students to opt in or out to having their work added to a public
units.policy: Instructors ask students to opt in or out of having their work added to a public database.

units.why: Principle 3 Guideline 1: if misuse is suspected, address it "from a collegial and collaborative perspective", i.e. talk with the student before escalating (P57).
units.anchor: these issues/questions from a collegial and collaborative perspective

units.why: "Do not use an accusatory/punitive tone in these conversations" is a separate prohibition on the manner of the suspected-misuse conversation (P57).

units.why: Guideline 2 asks instructors to "Promote and engage in open and ongoing dialogue with fellow faculty and staff" about AI, a peer-learning item (P63).

units.why: Principle 4 tells instructors to "Consider the issue of access and equity if you decide students can use AI", an equity item (P51).

units.why: The guideline asks whether "some students afford to pay for more advanced versions of AI that will give them unfair advantage", naming the paid-tool equity problem (P51).

units.why: Principle 5 says "Do not assume/apply a one-size fits all policy ... across all of your courses", so the AI rule is set per course by the instructor (P04).
units.anchor: Do not assume/apply a one-size fits all policy for students’ use of AI

units.why: Guideline 1 notes students "will be managing different AI expectations/permissions for their different classes", i.e. one course's rule does not carry over (P11).
units.anchor: those same students will be managing different AI expectations/permissions

units.why: Guideline 2 suggests that if a class allows a peer editor, "consider allowing Generative AI to fulfill this role", treating AI like a human collaborator (P45).
units.anchor: consider allowing Generative AI to fulfill this role

units.why: "continue scaffolding or breaking an assignment down to smaller components" where original work is required is an assignment-redesign suggestion (P35).
units.anchor: continue scaffolding or breaking an assignment down to smaller

units.why: Guideline 3 asks instructors to "Initiate and sustain conversations with your colleagues, department leadership" about generative AI limits, a faculty-community item (P63), separate from Principle 3 Guideline 2 which concerns dialogue with students.

units.why: Principle 6 says "You should consider not permitting the use of AI" for activities where writing is central, a prose-specific restriction (P18).
units.anchor: the use of AI for those in-class and homework activities

units.why: "Writing to learn is an intellectual activity that is crucial to the cognitive and social development of learners" gives the learning reason for limiting AI in writing (P41).

notes: Course layer deferred in collection; no school or computing unit policy found. Sample syllabus statements in the task force document are coded as units but are quoted examples from other institutions (Harvard, Salem State etc.), not App State rules; unit actors/modalities reflect the sample wording.
